title: Read SharePoint document version history with Microsoft Graph for audit evidence
summary: Graph requests to find a site, library and document and list file versions and list item versions, with paging, throttling handling, permissions and a PowerShell loop. Read-only, for audit preparation on controlled documents.
body:
## What it does

An auditor asks: "Show me every revision of this procedure and who changed it, and which version was current on 14 March." If your controlled documents live in a SharePoint document library, Microsoft Graph can answer that for one document or for a whole folder, and you can script it so the evidence package takes minutes instead of an afternoon of clicking through version history. These requests find the site and library, locate a document, list its versions with editor, time and size, and read the version history of the list item behind it, including the column values at each version.

This entry covers reading only. It does not restore, delete or change anything. It is a technical aid for audit preparation. What counts as an official revision, who approves, and how long you keep versions are defined in your quality system, not by the version numbers SharePoint assigns.

## Prerequisites

- An app registration or a signed-in admin identity with the read permissions listed below. Grant admin consent according to your tenant process. Test in Graph Explorer first.
- The document library must have versioning enabled. If versioning was off, there is no history to read. Versions may also be trimmed by retention settings; the documentation notes that previous versions may be kept for a limited time depending on admin settings.
- For the examples: host name `contoso.sharepoint.com`, site path `/sites/quality`, library `Controlled Documents`, file `WI-0815 Torque procedure.docx`. All of these are invented.

## Requests

Resolve the site from host name and relative path. The response contains the composite site id (host name, site collection id, site id):

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/contoso.sharepoint.com:/sites/quality
```

List the document libraries of that site and pick the drive by name:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/{site-id}/drives
```

Find the document by path inside a library (drive). Spaces in the path must be URL encoded (%20):

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/drives/{drive-id}/root:/Procedures/WI-0815%20Torque%20procedure.docx
```

For the default library of the site the shorter form works too:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/{site-id}/drive/root:/Procedures/WI-0815%20Torque%20procedure.docx
```

List the versions of the file. Versions come back newest first and `$orderby` is not supported:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/drives/{drive-id}/items/{item-id}/versions
```

Read the version history of the list item behind the document. This shows list column values (for example revision, status, owner) at each version, which is often what the auditor really asks for. You need the list id and the list item id. The driveItem resource page lists `listItem` as a relationship ("For drives in SharePoint, the associated document library list item"), so the request below is expected to work. The listItem-get page itself documents only the `/sites/{site-id}/lists/{list-id}/items/{item-id}` form, so test this drives form in Graph Explorer before you script it:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/drives/{drive-id}/items/{item-id}/listItem
```

The response of that call is a listItem; its `id` is the list item id. You also need the list id. The driveItem has a `sharepointIds` property that documents `listId`, `listItemId` and `siteId`; reading it with `GET .../drives/{drive-id}/items/{item-id}?$select=sharepointIds` is untested here, so test it first. Then read the item versions. The Learn pages show `?expand=fields` only on a single version (the example response there shows `fields` as an empty object, so check what your tenant returns); the list-versions page documents no query parameters. Treat `$expand=fields` on the collection as untested, and read single versions one by one if it fails:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/{site-id}/lists/{list-id}/items/{item-id}/versions
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/{site-id}/lists/{list-id}/items/{item-id}/versions/{version-id}?expand=fields
```

From a list item to its file when you start in the list:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/{site-id}/lists/{list-id}/items/{item-id}/driveItem
```

## Response shape

Versions of a file (driveItemVersion). The version id looks like "3.0":

```json
{
  "value": [
    {
      "id": "3.0",
      "lastModifiedBy": { "user": { "id": "[object-id]", "displayName": "Example Editor" } },
      "lastModifiedDateTime": "2026-03-14T12:34:53.912Z",
      "size": 123456
    },
    {
      "id": "2.0",
      "lastModifiedBy": { "user": { "id": "[object-id]", "displayName": "Example Editor" } },
      "lastModifiedDateTime": "2026-02-11T10:21:03.000Z",
      "size": 121004
    }
  ]
}
```

OneDrive and SharePoint do not preserve complete metadata for earlier versions, so some properties can be missing. Treat a missing value as "not available", not as "empty".

## Paging, errors and throttling

- If the response contains `@odata.nextLink`, call exactly that URL for the next page and repeat until it is absent. Do not extract the skip token yourself and do not rebuild the query.
- A page can contain zero or more items, and page sizes differ between APIs. The versions pages do not describe paging, so write the loop anyway.
- 429: wait for the number of seconds in the `Retry-After` header and retry; the throttling page says to use exponential backoff when the header is missing. Treat 503 the same way, although the pages used for this entry do not cover 503 specifically. Plan for it when you loop over hundreds of documents.
- 403: the identity lacks access to that site or library. Do not widen permissions to get around it; ask the site owner.
- 404: a wrong path, a renamed file, or a deleted item. Re-resolve by path.
- Log the `request-id` from the error body (it appears in `innerError` in the throttling example) together with the time of the call, so you can give it to Microsoft support if needed. Sending your own `client-request-id` header is a common practice, but the pages used here do not cover it, so check the Graph error documentation first.

A PowerShell loop using the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK (no secrets in the script, the sign-in is interactive):

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'Sites.Read.All' -NoWelcome
$uri = "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/drives/$driveId/items/$itemId/versions"
$versions = @()
while ($uri) {
    $resp = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET -Uri $uri
    $versions += $resp.value
    $uri = $resp.'@odata.nextLink'
}
$versions | ForEach-Object {
    [pscustomobject]@{
        Version  = $_.id
        Modified = $_.lastModifiedDateTime
        By       = $_.lastModifiedBy.user.displayName
        Size     = $_.size
    }
} | Export-Csv -Path .\versions.csv -NoTypeInformation -Encoding UTF8
```

## Worked example (invented data)

The auditor selects "WI-0815 Torque procedure.docx". The versions request returns 3.0 (2026-03-14), 2.0 (2026-02-11), 1.0 (2025-11-02). The question "which version was current on 14 March?" is answered by the newest version with a modified time on or before that day, in this case 3.0. The file versions page does not say whether the current version is the first entry of the list, so on one file compare the first entry with the `lastModifiedDateTime` of the driveItem itself before you rely on that reading. The list item versions show the `Revision` column changing from A to B at 2.0 and from B to C at 3.0, and the `Status` column at each point. Three versions in the file history and three revision letters is consistent here, but SharePoint creates a new version on many saves; five edits may produce five versions for one revision letter. The evidence is the pair (version, column values), not the version number alone.

## How to adapt

- A folder or a whole library: list children with `GET /drives/{drive-id}/root/children` and follow `@odata.nextLink`, then call the versions endpoint per file. Expect throttling for large libraries.
- Document metadata: the list item `fields` hold your own columns. Which column names you have is tenant-specific; read one item first.
- Different identity: delegated sign-in is the safest for an interactive audit; for a scheduled job use an app registration with a certificate, never a secret in the script.
- Narrower app permission: for per-site access look at the Sites.Selected model. Its overview describes grants on sites, lists, list items and files but does not say whether the versions endpoints accept it, and the versions pages list only Files.Read, Files.Read.All and Sites.Read.All. Test it with a pilot app registration before you plan on it.

## Required permissions

Documented on the pages used for this entry:

- File versions (driveItemVersion list): the page lists delegated Files.Read as least privileged and application Files.Read.All; higher privileged options include Files.Read.All and Sites.Read.All. Whether Files.Read is enough for a team-site library that the signed-in user did not create is not stated, so test it; the script below requests Sites.Read.All, which the page lists as higher privileged.
- List item versions (list and get): delegated and application Sites.Read.All (least), Sites.ReadWrite.All higher.
- Site by path: Sites.Read.All (least) for delegated and application. Drives of a site: Files.Read delegated and Files.Read.All application as least privileged, Sites.Read.All among the higher ones.
- So Sites.Read.All covers every call in this entry. Choose the least privileged option that works in your tenant and review the consent with your security team.

## Common mistakes

- Reading version numbers as official revisions. Draft saves and co-authoring create versions without any approval.
- Expecting versions to be there forever. Retention and version limits can remove older ones.
- Forgetting to URL encode spaces and special characters in the path.
- Using application permissions with tenant-wide read for a task that one person could do with delegated rights.
- Handing the raw CSV to the auditor without explaining the columns.

## Privacy and security

- The version list shows who edited when. That is personal data of employees; use it for audit evidence and not for performance review, and tell the works council or data protection officer about the purpose.
- Do not store tokens or exports in a shared folder. Delete the CSV when the audit is closed, or store it with the audit file under your retention rules.
- In aerospace and defence environments some documents are export controlled; confirm that the account and the machine running the script are allowed to touch them.

title: Read Teams Shifts schedules with Microsoft Graph to check shift coverage
summary: Read the schedule, scheduling groups and shifts of a Teams team with Graph, filter by date, count people per day against a minimum crew and handle UTC, drafts, paging and throttling. Read-only, with privacy notes.
body:
## What it does

Plants that plan shifts in the Shifts app of Microsoft Teams usually cannot answer a simple planning question without opening every team: how many people are scheduled per area and per shift next week, and where is the gap against the minimum crew? These requests read the schedule of a Teams team, its scheduling groups (for example "Hangar A" or "Line 3") and its shifts for a date window, so a script or a Power BI dataset can count coverage. Reading only; nothing is changed.

Shift data is planning data about people. Use it for capacity and coverage questions, not for individual monitoring. In many countries a works council has to agree before you evaluate it, and the data protection officer should know the purpose.

## Prerequisites

- The team uses the Shifts schedule. Check with `GET /teams/{teamId}/schedule` that the schedule exists and is provisioned. The response shows `enabled`, `timeZone` and `provisionStatus`, plus flags for open shifts, swap requests, offer requests, time off and the time clock.
- A signed-in identity with the delegated permission Schedule.Read.All, or an app registration with the application permission Schedule.Read.All. The documentation says this API supports admin permissions, which means an admin can read teams they are not a member of. Application permission means the app sees every team schedule in the tenant; check whether your tenant restricts that scope, and if you cannot restrict it, prefer delegated access with a dedicated reader account.
- This API is documented as available in the global cloud only, not in US Government or China clouds.
- Team ids: take them from the Teams admin center or from your team provisioning records (the team id equals the id of its Microsoft 365 group). Example ids below are placeholders.

## Requests

Read the schedule settings of a team:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/teams/{teamId}/schedule
```

Read the scheduling groups. They represent your areas or crews; each group carries a `displayName`, a list of `userIds`, an `isActive` flag and an optional `code`:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/teams/{teamId}/schedule/schedulingGroups
```

Read shifts. The documented example filters on both versions, with four comparisons (start and end of `sharedShift` and of `draftShift`). The request below filters on the shared version only, which the page does not show, so test it first; if it returns an error or nothing, use the documented four-comparison form, or read without a filter and filter in the script:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/teams/{teamId}/schedule/shifts?$filter=sharedShift/startDateTime ge 2026-11-23T00:00:00.000Z and sharedShift/endDateTime le 2026-11-30T00:00:00.000Z
```

The documentation states that `$filter` does not support the same property more than once in a query. So a range written as two comparisons on `sharedShift/startDateTime` fails; use one comparison on the start and one on the end, as above. Because both ends must lie inside the window, a shift that starts inside it but ends after it is not returned; widen the window by a day and cut it again in the script.

Resolve user ids from the shifts to names, one id per call or through JSON batching (the batching entry in this library shows the pattern). Check the permission first (see below):

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/users/{userId}?$select=id,displayName,mail
```

## Response shape

A shift contains `id`, `userId`, `schedulingGroupId`, `isStagedForDeletion`, `sharedShift` and `draftShift`. Both versions are shiftItem objects with `displayName`, `notes`, `startDateTime`, `endDateTime`, `theme` and `activities`. Times are in UTC. Draft changes are visible to managers only; the shared version is what employees see. The documentation also states that a shift cannot be shorter than 1 minute or longer than 24 hours. Example (shortened, invented values):

```json
{
  "value": [
    {
      "id": "SHFT_[guid]",
      "userId": "[user-object-id]",
      "schedulingGroupId": "TAG_[guid]",
      "isStagedForDeletion": false,
      "sharedShift": {
        "displayName": "Early",
        "startDateTime": "2026-11-23T05:00:00Z",
        "endDateTime": "2026-11-23T13:00:00Z",
        "theme": "blue",
        "activities": []
      },
      "draftShift": null
    }
  ]
}
```

## Paging, errors and throttling

- If a response contains `@odata.nextLink`, call that URL unchanged until it disappears. The shifts page does not describe paging, so write the loop anyway.
- Use the shared version for coverage counts. Where `sharedShift` is null the shift has not been shared yet and is not visible to employees, so decide explicitly whether draft shifts count.
- Shifts with `isStagedForDeletion` set to true are scheduled for removal when the schedule is shared; exclude them.
- 403 means missing permission or no admin permission; 404 usually means a wrong team id or no schedule; for 429 wait for `Retry-After` and retry with back off (treat 503 the same way; the pages used here do not cover it). Log the `request-id` of failed calls, and a `client-request-id` if you send one.
- Convert UTC to local time using the `timeZone` of the schedule, not the time zone of the machine running the script, and test the weeks around the clock change.

## Worked example (invented data)

Team "Hangar A", scheduling group "Line maintenance", week of 23 November 2026. The minimum crew your planner defined is 8 people per early shift (invented). The shifts request returns, after excluding drafts and staged deletions, early shifts per day: Monday 8, Tuesday 8, Wednesday 7, Thursday 8, Friday 6. Coverage is the count of distinct `userId` values with a shared shift starting between 05:00 and 07:00 UTC that day. Wednesday is one short, Friday two short: total gap 3 person-shifts (8 + 8 + 7 + 8 + 6 = 37 against 5 x 8 = 40). A PowerShell sketch for the count (sign-in is interactive, no secrets; it applies the same start window, and the window is an example, adapt it to your shift model):

```powershell
Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'Schedule.Read.All' -NoWelcome
$from = '2026-11-23T00:00:00.000Z'
$to   = '2026-11-30T00:00:00.000Z'
$uri  = "https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/teams/$teamId/schedule/shifts?`$filter=sharedShift/startDateTime ge $from and sharedShift/endDateTime le $to"
$shifts = @()
while ($uri) {
    $r = Invoke-MgGraphRequest -Method GET -Uri $uri
    $shifts += $r.value
    $uri = $r.'@odata.nextLink'
}
$shifts |
  Where-Object { $_.sharedShift -and -not $_.isStagedForDeletion } |
  Where-Object { $h = ([datetime]$_.sharedShift.startDateTime).ToUniversalTime().Hour; $h -ge 5 -and $h -lt 7 } |
  Group-Object { ([datetime]$_.sharedShift.startDateTime).ToUniversalTime().Date } |
  Select-Object @{n='Day';e={$_.Name}}, @{n='People';e={($_.Group.userId | Select-Object -Unique).Count}}
```

## How to adapt

- Per group counts: add `schedulingGroupId` to the grouping and map ids to names from the scheduling groups response.
- Qualification coverage (for example certifying staff per shift): Shifts does not hold qualifications. Keep a separate list or group and join on user id; do not invent a field in Shifts.
- Absences: time off is a separate resource of the schedule. This entry does not cover it, so check the Graph documentation for time off before you count absent people as present.
- Reporting: write the result into a SharePoint list or a dataset; never leave per-person shift data in an open workbook.

## Required permissions

- Schedule, scheduling groups, shifts (list): delegated Schedule.Read.All, application Schedule.Read.All. Higher privileged options listed on the pages: Schedule.ReadWrite.All, and for delegated also Group.Read.All and Group.ReadWrite.All.
- Resolve user names: the Get user page lists User.Read (own profile only) as least privileged for delegated access and User.Read.All for application access, with delegated User.ReadBasic.All among the higher options. Whether User.ReadBasic.All returns the properties you select (`mail`) is not stated there, so test it with your account.
- Do not grant write permissions for a reporting task.

## Common mistakes

- Filtering on the same property twice, which the documentation says is not supported.
- Reading UTC times as local times and miscounting night shifts that cross midnight.
- Counting draft shifts as committed.
- Using an application permission for the whole tenant when one team needs to be read.
- Presenting names and shifts to people who only need the totals.

## Privacy and security

- Shifts reveal when people work. Share totals by group and day, not names, unless a planner needs the names.
- Keep the app registration owner list short, rotate certificates, and never put secrets in scripts or in chat.
- Agree retention for exported data, and delete exports after the planning decision.

title: Create Planner tasks for corrective actions with Microsoft Graph, with checklist and duplicate check
summary: POST planner tasks for CAPA actions with assignments, due date and priority, then add description and checklist through task details with If-Match, plus ETag, limit and error handling and a duplicate check by reference number.
body:
## What it does

After a nonconformance, an audit finding or a customer complaint, the corrective and preventive actions (CAPA) have to be tracked: an owner, a due date, a verification step. Many quality teams do this in Planner because everybody already has it in Teams. These requests create a Planner task for each action from a script or a flow-like service, assign it, add a checklist (including the effectiveness check) and a description with the reference number, and avoid creating duplicates when the job runs twice.

Planner is a task tool, not a quality management system. The record of the nonconformance, the root cause and the closure decision belongs in your QMS. Use Planner for the follow-up and put the QMS reference into every task title, so both sides can be matched.

## Prerequisites

- A plan in a Microsoft 365 group (a team) with a bucket per workflow state, for example "Open actions", "In verification", "Closed". Read plan and bucket ids with the requests below.
- Permissions: delegated Tasks.ReadWrite for a signed-in user, or application Tasks.ReadWrite.All for an unattended job. The pages used here list Group.ReadWrite.All as a higher privileged delegated alternative; avoid it. For read-only checks the least privileged options are Tasks.Read (delegated) and Tasks.Read.All (application).
- The user ids (object ids) of the assignees. Look them up with `GET /users/{user-principal-name}` and read `id`.
- Planner limits: the Planner documentation says a 403 with codes such as MaximumTasksInProject, MaximumActiveTasksInProject, MaximumBucketsInProject or MaximumAssigneesInTasks means a service-defined limit was exceeded. The numbers are on the separate Planner limits page; check them for your tenant rather than assuming.

## Requests

Find the buckets of the plan:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/planner/plans/{plan-id}/buckets
```

Read the existing tasks of the plan to detect duplicates:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/planner/plans/{plan-id}/tasks
```

Create the task. `planId` is required; the example in the documentation uses `planId`, `bucketId`, `title` and `assignments`. Complex values such as an assignment must carry `@odata.type`, otherwise Planner returns 400:

```http
POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/planner/tasks
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "planId": "{plan-id}",
  "bucketId": "{bucket-id}",
  "title": "CAPA-2026-014 Update torque check in work instruction WI-0815",
  "dueDateTime": "2026-12-18T12:00:00Z",
  "priority": 3,
  "assignments": {
    "{assignee-object-id}": {
      "@odata.type": "#microsoft.graph.plannerAssignment",
      "orderHint": " !"
    }
  }
}
```

`dueDateTime` is in UTC. `priority` runs from 0 (highest) to 10 (lowest). The task resource page says Planner reads 0 and 1 as urgent, 2 to 4 as important, 5 to 7 as medium and 8 to 10 as low, and that Planner itself writes 1, 3, 5 and 9; use those four values so your tasks look like tasks created in the Planner app.

The task returns 201 Created with the new task, including its `id`. Description and checklist live in a separate object, task details. Read the details to get the ETag, then update with `If-Match`:

```http
GET https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/planner/tasks/{task-id}/details
```

The Planner overview describes etags as returned in the `@odata.etag` property of each resource. The sample on the details page does not show it, so check the actual response in your tenant and take the value from there. Then:

```http
PATCH https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/planner/tasks/{task-id}/details
Content-Type: application/json
Prefer: return=representation
If-Match: W/"[etag-value-from-the-read]"

{
  "description": "Source: NCR-2026-088. Root cause and decision are recorded in the QMS.",
  "checklist": {
    "[new-guid-1]": {
      "@odata.type": "microsoft.graph.plannerChecklistItem",
      "title": "Revise the work instruction and release the new revision",
      "isChecked": false
    },
    "[new-guid-2]": {
      "@odata.type": "microsoft.graph.plannerChecklistItem",
      "title": "Verify effectiveness after the period defined in your QMS",
      "isChecked": false
    }
  }
}
```

Each checklist key is a GUID you generate. With `Prefer: return=representation` you get 200 and the updated details, without it 204 and no body.

Update or close a task later with `PATCH /planner/tasks/{task-id}` and a new `If-Match`, for example `{ "percentComplete": 100 }`. A value of 100 means completed.

## Error handling

- 400: the Planner overview lists open-type properties without the right `@odata.type` (for example assignments), order hints in the wrong format (for example a value copied from a response) and logically inconsistent data such as a start date after the due date.
- 403: no permission, or one of the Planner limits above. The `code` in the error tells which limit.
- 404: the plan, bucket or task id does not exist, or the app cannot see it.
- 409 and 412: the ETag is stale. Read the resource again, take the new ETag, merge, retry. Every Planner PATCH and DELETE needs `If-Match` with the last known ETag.
- 429: wait for `Retry-After` and retry with back off (treat 503 the same way; the Planner pages do not cover it); create tasks one at a time with a short pause when you load many.
- Log the `request-id` from the error body for each failed call and keep the HTTP status and the error body; add a `client-request-id` header of your own only after checking the Graph error documentation.

## Idempotency

POST creates a new task every time. Put the QMS reference at the start of the title (`CAPA-2026-014`) and, before creating, check the task list of the plan for a title that starts with that reference. This is a client-side check; the plan tasks page documents no `$filter` and does not describe paging, so follow `@odata.nextLink` if it appears, and for large plans keep a local mapping of reference to task id instead.

## Worked example (invented data)

NCR-2026-088 produces three CAPA actions: revise a work instruction (owner A, due 2026-12-18), retrain two shifts (owner B, due 2026-12-11), add a gauge check to the setup sheet (owner C, due 2027-01-15). The script reads the plan's tasks, finds none starting with CAPA-2026-014, 015 or 016, and creates three tasks in the bucket "Open actions". It then reads each task's details, patches the description with the NCR reference and two checklist items. A rerun of the same script finds the three titles and creates nothing. Three creates, three detail reads and three detail patches are nine calls plus one plan read; at a few hundred milliseconds each, that is seconds, not minutes.

## How to adapt

- Several actions per NCR: add a counter suffix to the title (`CAPA-2026-014-1`).
- Moving a task to "In verification": `PATCH /planner/tasks/{task-id}` with the new `bucketId` and the current ETag.
- A flow instead of a script: the Planner connector in Power Automate does the same without custom code; use Graph when you need the checklist and details in one controlled step or run from a service.
- Categories (labels): the `appliedCategories` property can carry coloured labels, for example "Safety". The label names are defined on the plan; check the plan details before setting them.

## Common mistakes

- Setting `orderHint` from a value you got back, which the Planner overview names as a cause of 400. Keep the example value from the documentation (` !`) or read the Planner order hints article before you change it.
- Forgetting `@odata.type` on assignments or checklist items.
- Using the same GUID for two checklist items.
- Creating tasks with application permissions in a plan that the business owner does not know about. Agree the plan and its owners first.
- Closing the Planner task before the effectiveness check in the QMS is done.

## Privacy and security

- Assignee ids and due dates are personal data; keep the plan membership to the people involved in the corrective action.
- Do not write customer data or details of a person's mistake into titles. Reference the NCR number and describe the action, not the blame.
- For an unattended job use a certificate-based app registration, store no secrets in the script and give it only Tasks.ReadWrite.All. Review who may use that registration, and remember that application permissions work across all plans in the tenant that the service can reach.
